name: Tataltepec Chatino
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sullivant, John Ryan. 2015. The Phonology and Inflectional Morphology of Cháʔknyá, Tataltepec de Valdés Chatino, a Zapotecan Language. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin (hdl 2152/31493; UT repository via the Internet Archive capture 2022-01-24).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 sec. 2.2 'Stress', p. 54; sec. 2.2.1 'Phonological consequences of stress', p. 55 and fn. 1; Ch. 3 intro, p. 68; sec. on /β̞/, p. 126; Ch. 4 intro, p. 150.
catalog_quote: All syllables in Tataltepec Chatino are either stressed (σS) or unstressed (σW). Stressed syllables are always stem-final syllables (that is, word-final unless the stem is followed by one or more enclitics), and stem-final syllables are always stressed. ... Tataltepec Chatino and the other languages of Core Chatino (Zenzontepec Chatino and all extant topolects of Eastern Chatino) all share this stem-final stress where disyllabic stems ω are realized as σW σS. Beyond phonetic affects of stress (including greater durations and intensities of σS), there are phonological consequences of stress. Only σS can be long or linked to the [+ nasal] feature, while σW can only be oral and short. ... Each stem is associated with one lexical tone class (which contains a sequence of zero to two tones) and contains one stressed syllable. Person clitics can have their own tone class, but form a phonological constituent with their host in that they do not receive sentence-level stress. Stressed syllables are the stem-final syllables where the number of phonemic contrasts is greatest. By contrast, unstressed syllables are the penultimate and antepenultimate (or earlier) syllables where the range of possible phonemic contrasts is reduced.
world_status: statement found in an open source

At the stated locator (the text layerprinted p.54, section 2.2 'Stress') the text reads exactly: 'All syllables in Tataltepec Chatino are either stressed (σS) or unstressed (σW). Stressed syllables are always stem-final syllables (that is, word-final unless the stem is followed by one or more enclitics), and stem-final syllables are always stressed.' The second half of the quote (after the compiler [..]) is v…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the stem, which is the final syllable of the word unless enclitics (e.g. person clitics) follow; enclitics are unstressed and outside the stress domain. Each stem has exactly one stressed syllable; penultimate and earlier syllables are unstressed and show reduced contrasts (no length, no nasality, few mid vowels). Spanish loans are restressed on the final syllable regardless of source stress. The language is also tonal (lexical tone sequences linked right-to-left from the stressed final mora).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; each stem 'contains one stressed syllable'. In verb compounds the first stem loses its stress (its long vowel shortens), so only the final syllable of the compound is stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics (person clitics) do not take stress, so stress is stem-final rather than strictly word-final in cliticized forms; compound verbs have a single stress on the last stem; loans receive final stress. Footnote: non-Core Chatino Zapotecan languages (Soltec, Teojomulco Chatino) had the opposite stem-initial pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem/phonological word (ω): stress is stem-final = word-final absent enclitics; clitics form a phonological constituent with the host but are unstressed. Statement is phonological (distributional evidence from length/nasality licensing and compounding) with mention of phonetic correlates (duration, intensity); tone is independent and lexical.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes exactly Tataltepec de Valdés Chatino (Cháʔknyá), glottocode tata1258 / ISO cta; Sullivant notes no prominent internal dialect variation. The same stem-final stress is stated to hold for all Core Chatino (Zenzontepec zenz1235 and Eastern Chatino topolects).

tone_statements.quote: Hilaria Cruz, Eric Campbell, and Tony used this method on their first visit to Tataltepec (TAT) (Figure 1). Like ZAC and ZEN, TAT preserves most of the prosodic divisions shown in Table 6. As the pictures show, ten columns of cards were created, even though the isolation tonal distinctions in question reduced to just three categories, H, L, and null (Sullivant & Woodbury 2009; Sullivant 2013), regardless of mora count. ... The languages, as we have seen, are all tonally rich. They all divide the lexicon into many classes, based on the tone or tonal sequence; and they link individual tones to moras.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.2 Method B, p. 504 + sec. 6 Conclusions, p. 520
tone_statements.summary: Three isolation categories H, L, null counted by the source (null = toneless, so two specified tones); analysis credited to Sullivant & Woodbury 2009, Sullivant 2013; TAT has extensive sandhi; no TAT forms shown.

tone_statements.citation: Sullivant, John Ryan. 2013. The tones of Tataltepec Chatino. Paper presented at the SSILA Winter Meeting, Boston, 4 January 2013. PowerPoint ('2013-SSILA-TAT_tone_presentation-final-jrs.pptx') with linked wav audio files, distributed by the Chatino Language Documentation Project (Google Drive folder 'Sullivant_John-2013-SSILA').
tone_statements.quote: Like nearly every Otomanguean language, TC is has lexical tone and like other Chatino languages, the tone system is fairly complex. ... the tone bearing unit for TC is the stem, that is, tone is not assigned independently per syllable, but complex tones can be associated with one stem, and even one monomoraic vowel. ... TC uses four tone formatives Low Mid High and Superhigh to produce its tone sequences. A stem may be linked to at most two tone formatives, and need not be linked to any tone formatives.
tone_statements.locator: speaker notes attached to slides 3, 7 and 9; inventory on slide 9 'Inventory of Tone Formatives' (l.75-80) and slides 15/40 'Tone Sequence Inventory'
tone_statements.summary: 4 level formatives (+ unmarked X) form 8 stem-level tone sequences (X, 0+X, L, 0+L, M, H, 0, 0L); the 'unlinked' superhigh links only after L/H and is 'not truly floating'; F0 tracks per sequence.

tone_statements.quote: Tataltepec Chatino is a language with a complex system of lexical tone in which words may be distinguished by movements in fundamental frequency alone. The latest analysis of the tone system of this language identifies five non-sandhi-derived tones which may appear in isolation: Relaxed, Low, High, High-High and High-Low (Sullivant and Woodbury 2009). The tones are stem-linked and each tone extends over the entire word. ... (as well as the at least two sandhi-derived tones which occur in limited contexts)
tone_statements.locator: p.1 Introduction and p.1-2 across the page break
tone_statements.summary: Five isolation tones (Relaxed, Low, High, High-High, High-Low), stem-linked, spread over the whole word; 'at least two' more sandhi-derived tones unnamed. Perception pilot on High vs Low (koó vs koò).

tone_statements.citation: Sullivant, J. Ryan & Anthony C. Woodbury. 2009. El tono y el sandhi de tono en el chatino de Tataltepec de Valdés. In Las memorias del Congreso de Idiomas Indígenas de Latinoamérica-IV (CILLA IV). Austin: Archive of the Indigenous Languages of Latin America, University of Texas at Austin. 10 pp.http://www.ailla.utexas.org/site/cilla4/Sullivant_Woodbury_CILLA_IV.pdf(open copy = 2012 revision distributed by the Chatino Language Documentation Project: 'Este manuscrito se revisa por publicación en 2012'). [Title on the paper itself reads 'sandhi de tono', not 'del tono' as in Sullivant 2015's reference list.]
tone_statements.quote: En el lexicón, cada categoría tonal se representa por una secuencia de tonos que se asocian a bases enteras ... Así mostramos que el chatino de Tataltepec de Valdés tiene siete tonos, de los cuales, cinco se distinguen en la superficie (Relajado, Alto, Bajo, Alto-Relajado, Alto-Bajo) y dos pares de tonos se distinguen por su comportamiento en entornos de sandhi (los Relajados receptivos y normales junto con los Bajos receptivos y normales).
tone_statements.translation: In the lexicon, each tonal category is represented by a sequence of tones that associate to whole bases ... Thus we show that the Chatino of Tataltepec de Valdés has seven tones, of which five are distinguished on the surface (Relaxed, High, Low, High-Relaxed, High-Low) and two pairs of tones are distinguished by their behaviour in sandhi environments (the receptive and normal Relaxed together with the receptive and normal Low).
tone_statements.locator: Section 4 'Resumen, y una propuesta para la representación de los tonos' (pages unnumbered)
tone_statements.summary: 7 word-level tone classes from H, L, toneless moras and a floating H; Alto-Bajo/Alto-Relajado 'complex tones' analysed as H-L / H-X sequences; f0 plots, minimal sets, sandhi frames. Forms: 100+.

tone.translation: In the lexicon, each tonal category is represented by a sequence of tones that associate to whole bases ... Thus we show that the Chatino of Tataltepec de Valdés has seven tones, of which five are distinguished on the surface (Relaxed, High, Low, High-Relaxed, High-Low) and two pairs of tones are distinguished by their behaviour in sandhi environments (the receptive and normal Relaxed together with the receptive and normal Low).
